items.title: Add AbortLink to cancel browser operations with a CancellationToken

labels.name: community-contribution
labels.description: Indicates that the PR has been added by a community member

items.body:
- [x] You've read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE-OF-CONDUCT.md).
- [x] You've included unit or integration tests for your change, where applicable.
- [x] You've included inline docs for your change, where applicable.
- [x] There's an open issue for the PR that you are making. If you'd like to propose a new feature or change, please open an issue to discuss the change or find an existing issue.

Add AbortLink to cancel browser operations with a CancellationToken

## Description

This implements the design in #70044. It adds the internal `AbortLink`, the factory that creates it, and their tests. The public API does not change, and no family uses `AbortLink` yet. The first one will be Fetch (#69882), and its proposal (#70046) already builds on this design. With this merged first, the Fetch PR can use the real type. The open question in #70044 (a small function in the JS module of the package to save round trips) does not block this PR, because it would change only internals.

### AbortLinkFactory and AbortLink

`FeatureContext.AbortLinkFactory` is an `AbortLinkFactory` shared by the scope. A projection receives it when it is created, as it receives `CreateEventListenerCollection()`. For each operation, the family calls `CreateAsync(cancellationToken)`. It creates a browser `AbortController` with `InvokeConstructorAsync`, reads its `signal` as an object reference, and registers a callback on the token that calls `abort()`. The family passes `Signal` to the browser operation, and calls the operation through `IJSRuntime` with `CancellationToken.None`. The issue explains why.

A few details are worth a look.

- The two setup calls (the constructor and `signal`) use the overloads without a token, so they keep the default interop timeout. Only the browser operation itself runs with `CancellationToken.None`.
- `CreateAsync` returns `null` for a token that cannot be canceled, so a call without a token costs nothing. For a token that is already canceled, or after the scope has ended, it throws before any interop call.
- If the token is canceled or the scope ends while the setup calls run, `CreateAsync` disposes both references and throws, before it registers the callback. If the token is canceled just before `Register`, `Register` runs the callback at once, so the abort is not lost.
- The factory keeps the links that are still open. When the scope ends, `FeatureContext` disposes the factory, and the factory disposes those links, so their callbacks leave the tokens. A token that outlives the circuit can no longer keep the circuit alive through an operation that never ended. A failure there is logged, because scope disposal does not throw.
- The callback runs on the thread that cancels the token. It sends `abort()` and changes no state, so it needs no lock. It ignores `JSDisconnectedException` (the circuit is gone, and the operation with it) and logs any other failure.
- Everything else runs on the scope's synchronization context, as in the event listener code, so there is no `ConfigureAwait(false)` and the list of open links has no lock.
- `DisposeAsync` removes the link from the factory and the callback from the token first. `CancellationTokenRegistration.DisposeAsync` waits for a callback that is running, so no `abort()` goes to a disposed reference. It then disposes the two references, the signal also when releasing the controller fails. `JSObjectReference.DisposeAsync` already ignores `JSDisconnectedException`, so `DisposeAsync` has no `catch`.
- `FeatureContext` keeps the factory in a field typed as `IInternalAsyncDisposal`, as it does for the callback factory of events, so an app that never cancels a browser operation does not keep the type.
- `CreateCanceledException` builds the `OperationCanceledException` that a family throws when its interop call fails after the token was canceled. It keeps the browser error as `InnerException`.

### Tests

- `AbortLinkTest` has 16 unit tests that go through `FeatureContext` with a recording fake. The fake leaves the overloads with a token unimplemented, so a call that passes a token fails the test. The tests cover the token that cannot be canceled, the canceled token, cancellation during setup, a failing setup, disposal (also when releasing the controller fails), the release of open links at the end of the scope (once only, and also when the scope ends during setup), a closed circuit and another failure of `abort()`, and `CreateCanceledException`.
- `AbortLinkTests` has 3 E2E tests in both render modes. A small feature in the test app calls `fetch` the way a family would, and gets itself with `Window.GetOrAddFeature` and `context.AbortLinkFactory`. The test app server holds a request until the browser aborts it, and records what happened. The tests wait for that record through a request that the server answers when the state is reached, so no step depends on a delay. They cover a request that is left alone, an abort before the headers (canceled from a thread pool thread, as a timer does) and while the body is read, and a token that is already canceled, for which no request is sent. The page uses the result marker of the other E2E tests.
- All 105 unit tests of the package pass. All 16 E2E tests of the package pass with `dotnet run` and from the output of `dotnet publish`. When I removed the `abort()` call from `AbortLink`, `AbortLink_AbortsTheRequestInTheBrowserWhenTheTokenIsCanceled` failed, so the test depends on the real abort. The E2E tests run in Chromium only.
- The release at the end of the scope has the same kind of check. Without the loop in `AbortLinkFactory`'s disposal, `ScopeDisposal_ReleasesTheLinksStillOpen` fails. Without the `_disposed` check after the setup calls, `CreateAsync_ThrowsAndReleasesTheReferencesWhenTheScopeEndsDuringCreation` fails.
- In a trimmed WebAssembly app that never uses `context.AbortLinkFactory`, `AbortLink`, `AbortLinkFactory`, and their log messages are removed. Only the `FeatureContext` field stays, as the field for the callback factory of events does.

### What I checked in other browsers

Before this PR, I checked the idea in a scratch app that is not in this PR. It calls `fetch` through plain `IJSRuntime` calls, and its server records whether the browser aborted each request. I ran it in Interactive Server and WebAssembly, in Chromium, Firefox, and the WebKit build that Playwright ships for Windows. The results were the same in all six.

| Scenario | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Token passed to `IJSRuntime` only | .NET throws `TaskCanceledException`, but the server request runs to completion. |
| `abort()` while waiting for the headers | `fetch` rejects at once and the server sees the abort. |
| `abort()` after `fetch` resolved, while `text()` reads the body | `text()` rejects and the server sees the abort. |
| Signal that is already aborted | `fetch` rejects at once and no request reaches the server. |
| `abort()` from `token.Register` in Interactive Server | Works, also when the callback runs outside the circuit's sync context. |
| Error text of an abort | Chromium "signal is aborted without reason" (and "The user aborted a request." while reading the body), Firefox "The operation was aborted.", WebKit "Fetch is aborted". WebKit ignores a reason passed to `abort()`. |

The error text differs by browser, so `AbortLink` never reads it. A family decides by `token.IsCancellationRequested`.

Contributes to #70044

items.title: Reuse RenderBatchWriter across render batches in RemoteRenderer
items.body:
# Reuse RenderBatchWriter across render batches in RemoteRenderer

- [x] You've read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE-OF-CONDUCT.md).
- [x] You've included unit or integration tests for your change, where applicable.
- [x] You've included inline docs for your change, where applicable.
- [ ] There's an open issue for the PR that you are making. (Follow-up to review feedback on #70125.)

Stop allocating a new batch writer and stream for every Blazor Server render batch.

## Description

Follow-up to @pavelsavara's suggestion on #70125. `RemoteRenderer.UpdateDisplayAsync` created a new `ArrayBuilderMemoryStream`, `RenderBatchWriter`, `BinaryWriter`, string `ArrayBuilder` and dedup `Dictionary` for every render batch. This PR keeps one writer per renderer and points its stream at each batch's own output buffer.

On the real `RemoteRenderer.UpdateDisplayAsync` + ack path, this halves allocations for a small interactive update (776 → 392 B) and cuts time by about 8%.

**Why this is safe**
- Each batch still gets its own `ArrayBuilder<byte>` output buffer. That buffer is kept in the unacknowledged-batch queue until the client acks it, so it is never shared or reused.
- `UpdateDisplayAsync` runs on the renderer's dispatcher, and `Renderer` guards it with `_isBatchInProgress`, so a renderer never writes two batches at once. The writer belongs to one renderer, so nothing is shared across circuits.
- `RenderBatchWriter.Write` now resets its string table in a `finally`, including when a write throws. Between batches the writer holds no strings, and its string `ArrayBuilder` has returned its array to the pool. So the renderer never needs to dispose it, and a dispose racing a render can't return a buffer that is still in use.
- If a batch used more than 128 deduplicated strings, the dictionary is replaced instead of cleared, so one large render doesn't leave a big table alive for the rest of the circuit.
- The wire format and the WebAssembly/WebView callers are unchanged, and there are no public API changes.

**Tests:** two new `RenderBatchWriterTest` cases reuse one writer for two batches, one of them after a failed write. Both fail on `main`, where the second batch's string table still holds the first batch's strings, and pass here. Server (396), WebView (16) and WebAssembly (56) unit tests pass locally.

### Benchmark

BenchmarkDotNet, in-process. The benchmark drives the real path: `RemoteRenderer.UpdateDisplayAsync(batch)` followed by `OnRenderCompletedAsync(batchId)`, with an offline client so no SignalR send. The batches are the same as in #70125's `RenderBatchWriterBenchmark` (a 5-edit counter-style update, and a 200-row table initial render). I ran 3 interleaved rounds (main, PR, main, PR, main, PR) on a 2-core Linux VM.

| Method | main R1 / R2 / R3 | PR R1 / R2 / R3 | Δ time | Allocated main → PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Small batch | 829.6 / 864.6 / 819.8 ns | 778.2 / 792.1 / 750.5 ns | **−7.7%** | **776 B → 392 B (−49%)** |
| Large batch | 97.9 / 96.4 / 96.4 µs | 93.6 / 94.8 / 93.4 µs | **−3.1%** | **5,032 B → 4,401 B (−13%)** |

<details><summary>Benchmark harness (throwaway; not part of this PR)</summary>

A console project inside the repo with `AssemblyName=Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Server.Tests` (for internals access), referencing Server and SignalR.Core, and using `InProcessEmitToolchain` + `MemoryDiagnoser`:

```csharp
[GlobalSetup] // options = new CircuitOptions(); jsRuntime = new RemoteJSRuntime(...); services registers IJSRuntime
_renderer = new BenchRenderer(services, options, jsRuntime); // RemoteRenderer subclass, offline CircuitClientProxy
_nextBatchId = 2; // RemoteRenderer pre-increments _nextRenderId = 1

private Task RenderAndAck(in RenderBatch batch)
{
    var task = _renderer.Update(in batch);              // => UpdateDisplayAsync(in batch)
    _renderer.OnRenderCompletedAsync(_nextBatchId++, null); // dequeues + disposes the batch buffer
    if (!task.IsCompleted) { throw new InvalidOperationException("Batch was not acknowledged."); }
    return task;
}
```
</details>

This is independent of #70125 (which changes how frames and edits are encoded); both touch `RenderBatchWriter.cs` but in different methods.

### Follow-up: `IpcSender` (WebView) and `WebAssemblyRenderer` (7e0ca8700a)

At reviewer request, the same reuse is applied to the other two `RenderBatchWriter` call sites:

- **`IpcSender.ApplyRenderBatch`** (WebView): the writer and stream are cached in a private field. Each batch takes them with `Interlocked.Exchange` and puts them back in `finally`, so two concurrent callers can never share them; if the cache is empty, a new writer is created. The per-batch `ArrayBuilder<byte>` is now also disposed (returned to the pool) in `finally`, once the base64 message string has copied its contents. On `main` it was never disposed.
- **`WebAssemblyRenderer.UpdateDisplayOutOfProcess`**: the writer and stream are cached in fields (the renderer is single-threaded) and retargeted at each batch's own `ArrayBuilder`. The existing `finally { arrayBuilder.Dispose(); }` is unchanged.

**WebView `IpcSender.ApplyRenderBatch`**: real path. BenchmarkDotNet, 3 interleaved rounds, mean of each round:

| Batch | main R1/R2/R3 | PR R1/R2/R3 | Allocated |
|---|---|---|---|
| Small | 1.860* / 1.252 / 1.288 µs | 1.048 / 1.041 / 1.061 µs | 5 KB → 3 KB |
| Large | 438.2 / 404.1 / 412.5 µs | 420.8 / 424.1 / 396.6 µs (noise) | 509 KB → 445 KB |

\*R1 main small had high variance (median 1.273 µs).

**WebAssembly out-of-process sequence**: the real `UpdateDisplayOutOfProcess` needs browser JS interop, so this benchmark reproduces its exact serialize + `ToArray` steps (UTF-16 string table) on CoreCLR, main pattern vs PR pattern:

| Batch | main R1/R2/R3 | PR R1/R2/R3 | Allocated |
|---|---|---|---|
| Small | 567.4 / 558.7 / 552.0 ns | 490.5 / 496.8 / 485.1 ns (−12%) | 880 B → 496 B |
| Large | 102.6 / 101.7 / 102.7 µs | 99.4 / 120.3* / 99.0 µs (noise) | 70,457 B → 69,825 B |

\*outlier round.

Tests: Components.Server 396, Components.WebView 16 and Components.WebAssembly 56 all pass.

**🤖 Posted by ASP.NET Core Perf 2 (AI Agent)**

items.title: [Validation] Blazor Hybrid teardown while JavaScript calls are in flight

labels.name: Validation
labels.description: This issue is used to track validation efforts

labels.name: validation-scenario
labels.description: This issue describes a validation testing scenario

items.body:
**Scenario contact:** @javiercn

## Scenario

**This scenario validates that a fix works.** A native app hosting Blazor is closed, backgrounded and navigated around far more abruptly than a web page, and its components are often in the middle of talking to JavaScript when that happens. Disposing an `IJSObjectReference` after the WebView had gone threw `JSDisconnectedException`, which showed up as hangs on teardown and alarming errors in the debug output. Navigation and disposal now mark the JS runtime disconnected before components are disposed, and that exception is caught and discarded.

This validates that a Hybrid app tears down cleanly.

## Minimum build

.NET 11 Preview 7 or later.

## Configurations to cover

* Blazor Web App
  * [ ] Static SSR
  * [ ] Interactive Server
  * [ ] Interactive WebAssembly
  * [ ] Interactive Auto
* [ ] Standalone WebAssembly
* [x] Hybrid (MAUI)

## Also exercise

* [ ] Published output
* [ ] An existing .NET 10 app upgraded to .NET 11
* [ ] Trimming or ahead-of-time compilation
* [ ] More than one server instance, or a proxy in front
* [ ] Hot Reload
* [ ] An IDE as well as the command line
* [ ] Container

## Setup

You need the workloads for building a native app for at least one platform, and a device or emulator. Covering more than one platform is worthwhile, since the embedded browser differs between them.

## What to build

A native app hosting Blazor, with pages that are busy in ways that make teardown awkward. Include a page that keeps a JavaScript module loaded and calls into it repeatedly, one that starts a slow JavaScript call and does not wait for it, one with a timer that keeps firing, and one that has registered .NET methods for JavaScript to call back into. Give the components proper cleanup so you can tell whether it runs. Add a native page alongside the Blazor content so you can move between the two kinds of screen, and log to the debug output when each component is cleaned up.

## Things to try

* Navigating away from each busy page while it is mid-flight.
* Moving from a Blazor screen to a native screen and back, repeatedly.
* Closing the app while a page is in the middle of a JavaScript call.
* Backgrounding the app and returning to it, and backgrounding it and then closing it.
* Using the operating system's back gesture or button rather than in-app navigation.
* Rotating the device while a page is busy.
* Repeating the cycle many times in one session and watching memory.
* Watching the debug output throughout for exceptions and warnings.

## Expected behavior

Teardown completes promptly however busy the page was, and calls that were already in flight go quietly.

### Must hold

* Leaving each busy page runs its cleanup and does not hang.
* Closing the app while a JavaScript call is in flight terminates promptly rather than waiting on work that will never finish.
* No exception from calls that were in flight appears in the debug output. In particular, disposing a JavaScript object reference after the connection is gone must not surface a `JSDisconnectedException`.
* Repeated moves between Blazor and native screens leave memory stable across the session.
* Returning from the background finds the app in a working state.

### Expected differences between configurations

* The embedded browser differs between platforms, so cover more than one if you can. A teardown that is clean on one platform and not on another is a finding.

## Documentation to use

* [ASP.NET Core Blazor Hybrid](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/blazor/hybrid/?view=aspnetcore-11.0)
* [Component disposal](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/blazor/components/component-disposal?view=aspnetcore-11.0)

## What to report

Report results using the format described in the [validation testing manual](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/68479). Include link to a repository with the test app.

> [!NOTE]
> **Disclaimer:** This validation scenario may have been written with AI assistance and may contain errors. It is a testing aid, not an official specification of intended behavior or security guarantees. Its expectations alone do not establish a bug or vulnerability. Verify suspected issues independently against official documentation and reproducible product behavior before reporting them.

### Describe the bug I have a Blazor Server app that uses Windows Authentication. It requires SignalR hub connection to update partial UI when a user click a button. I have followed [Use ASP.NET Core SignalR with Blazor WebAssembly](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/tutorials/signalr-blazor-webassembly?view=aspnetcore-3.1&tabs=visual-studio) documentation as well read [#22767](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/22767) and tried following [SignalR cross-origin negotiation for authentication](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/blazor/fundamentals/additional-scenarios?view=aspnetcore-3.1#signalr-cross-origin-negotiation-for-authentication). The following code works when debugging locally on IIS Express using Visual Studio 2019 Enterprise but it returns 401 Unauthorized exception while starting hub connection when it's deployed to IIS, **especially when** it has subdomain binding (http://subdomain.mydomain.org). **It only works when navigating via server name and port number "http://servername:60006"**. Please note that the signalr hub are hosted along with Blazor server app so there is no cross origin. **NavMenu.razor** ```csharp @using Microsoft.AspNetCore.SignalR.Client @inject NavigationManager NavigationManager @implements IDisposable

items.body:
Hello,

We are getting the following error below when trying to use ProtectedBrowserStorage with blazor on .NET 6.0 (and 5.0) on IIS 10.  I've tried making 'load profile' = true in the app pool settings, but no luck. 

Error: System.Security.Cryptography.CryptographicException: The key {#redacted#} was not found in the key ring. For more information go to http://aka.ms/dataprotectionwarning
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection.KeyManagement.KeyRingBasedDataProtector.UnprotectCore(Byte[] protectedData, Boolean allowOperationsOnRevokedKeys, UnprotectStatus& status)
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection.KeyManagement.KeyRingBasedDataProtector.Unprotect(Byte[] protectedData)
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection.DataProtectionCommonExtensions.Unprotect(IDataProtector protector, String protectedData)
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Server.ProtectedBrowserStorage.ProtectedBrowserStorage.Unprotect[TValue](String purpose, String protectedJson)
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Server.ProtectedBrowserStorage.ProtectedBrowserStorage.GetAsync[TValue](String purpose, String key)

Thank you,
J

items.title: InputFile Component

labels.name: api-approved
labels.description: API was approved in API review, it can be implemented

items.body:
### Summary
- Migrated `InputFile` from https://github.com/SteveSandersonMS/BlazorInputFile to `M.A.C.Web.Extensions`
- Removed dependency on third-party base64 encoding JS code.
- Added `IJSUnmarshalledRuntime` to allow `RemoteFileListEntryStream` to make unmarshalled JS invocations without reflection.
- Reimplemented `RemoteFileListEntryStream` to use `System.IO.Pipelines`.
- Added E2E tests

Addresses #12205
